question: What is osteomyelitis?

options.A: An autoimmune destruction of bone lining
options.B: A malignant tumor originating in the marrow
options.C: A degenerative softening of the cartilage joints
options.D: An infection of the bone and bone marrow

explanation: Osteomyelitis is simply an infection that gets inside the bone and its inner marrow. You've got this!

question: Why does swelling inside an infected bone cause bone tissue to die?

options.A: It causes the surrounding muscle tissue to pull the bone apart
options.B: It crushes the local blood vessels and cuts off the oxygen supply
options.C: It neutralizes all calcium stores within the hard outer matrix
options.D: It instantly triggers massive white blood cell suicide throughout the shaft

explanation: Bones are super hard and cannot stretch! When swelling happens inside, pressure builds up and pinches off the blood vessels, meaning no oxygen gets through to keep the tissue alive.

question: Which bacterium is most commonly responsible for causing osteomyelitis?
explanation: Staph aureus is the heavy hitter behind most bone and joint infections. A great microbe to keep top of mind for your exams!

question: How does hematogenous osteomyelitis differ from contiguous osteomyelitis?

options.A: Hematogenous only affects the skull, while contiguous affects long bones exclusively
options.B: Hematogenous is caused by viruses, whereas contiguous is always caused by fungi
options.C: Hematogenous spreads through the bloodstream, while contiguous comes from a nearby open wound or infection
options.D: Hematogenous occurs only in older adults, while contiguous is strictly pediatric

explanation: Think of 'hematogenous' as hitching a ride through the blood from somewhere else in the body, while 'contiguous' means the infection touched the bone directly from an outside wound nearby.

question: What is the main feature that separates chronic osteomyelitis from acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: The complete inability of bacteria to cause tissue damage
options.B: The duration of the infection lasting for months or years
options.C: The restriction of the disease to flat facial bones
options.D: The total absence of any pain or localized swelling

explanation: The big difference is time! Chronic means it has been hanging around stubbornly for months or even years.

question: A patient has an infected open leg fracture that hasn't healed over the past eight months, despite short courses of oral antibiotics. What type of osteomyelitis is this?
explanation: When an infection sticks around for many months and fights off standard treatments, it has turned into chronic osteomyelitis.

question: Which symptom is a classic sign of chronic osteomyelitis?

options.A: Instantaneous paralysis of the affected limb
options.B: A sudden high fever with no local pain whatsoever
options.C: Complete numbness and coldness in the toes
options.D: A draining sinus tract leaking pus onto the skin

explanation: A sinus tract is a little tunnel that forms from the infected bone out to the skin, constantly draining pus. A classic clinical clue!

question: Why might an elderly patient with osteomyelitis not have a high fever?

options.A: Circulating antibiotics constantly suppress core body temperature
options.B: Their immune response may be blunted, altering classic systemic signs
options.C: Bone infections never cause systemic temperature changes in adults
options.D: Older bones are completely immune to inflammatory pyrogens

explanation: Older adults sometimes have quieter immune systems, meaning they might not show the textbook high fever even when a serious infection is brewing.

question: Which imaging test is the gold standard for catching a bone infection early?
explanation: X-rays take a while to show bone changes, but an MRI can spot early bone marrow changes and swelling super fast!

question: Why do nurses monitor blood inflammatory markers like ESR and CRP in osteomyelitis patients?

options.A: To measure the exact amount of calcium left in the bone shaft
options.B: To track how well the body is responding to treatment over time
options.C: To prove that the infection started from a dental cavity
options.D: To determine whether the patient needs an immediate blood transfusion

explanation: ESR and CRP go up when there's inflammation and drop back down as the patient gets better. They are great tools to see if our treatments are working!

question: What is the typical length of antibiotic treatment for osteomyelitis?

options.A: Four to six weeks or longer

explanation: Because it's tricky for drugs to get deep inside hard bone tissue, patients need a nice long course of antibiotics—usually 4 to 6 weeks or even more.

question: A patient goes home with a PICC line for long-term IV antibiotics. Why use a central line here?

options.A: It safely accommodates prolonged, concentrated intravenous drug therapy outside the hospital
options.B: It prevents the patient from moving their arm during physical therapy
options.C: It allows nurses to directly irrigate the bone marrow every few minutes
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for any subsequent blood tests

explanation: A PICC line lets patients receive weeks of strong IV antibiotics safely at home without constantly getting poked in their regular arm veins.

question: What is the main goal of surgical debridement in osteomyelitis?

options.A: To fuse the adjacent joints together permanently
options.B: To stretch the limb to make it longer
options.C: To replace all marrow with synthetic polymers
options.D: To remove dead and infected bone tissue

explanation: Debridement is basically a clean-up operation where the surgeon scrapes away all the dead, infected bone that antibiotics alone can't reach.

question: Why do surgeons sometimes place antibiotic beads right inside a bone cavity after cleaning it out?

options.A: To stimulate rapid hair growth around the surgical incision
options.B: To act as permanent replacement for missing bone mineral
options.C: To permanently block blood flow and prevent further swelling
options.D: To deliver high concentrations of medication directly to the infected site

explanation: Those little beads release a high dose of medicine right where it's needed most, straight into the bone pocket while keeping the rest of the body safe.

question: What is a super important piece of discharge teaching for a patient on antibiotics for a bone infection?

options.A: Switch to topical creams once the IV line is removed
options.B: Stop taking the drugs the moment pain subsides
options.C: Double the dose if a fever returns for one evening
options.D: Finish the entire prescription even if symptoms disappear

explanation: Always remind patients to finish every single pill! Stopping early can let the stubborn bacteria bounce back stronger.

question: While checking a patient with a leg infection, you notice their toes are cool, pale, and slow to refill with blood. What is your best first move?

options.A: Apply a heating pad directly to the toes
options.B: Document the findings as normal post-surgical swelling
options.C: Encourage the patient to get out of bed and walk
options.D: Report the neurovascular changes to the physician immediately

explanation: Cool, pale toes with a sluggish refill mean blood flow is in trouble (or compartment syndrome is setting in). Always report this to the doctor right away!

question: What is a major, life-threatening complication that can happen if bone infections are left untreated?

options.A: Permanent vision loss in both eyes

explanation: When an infection escapes the bone and enters the bloodstream, it can cause a whole-body emergency known as sepsis. Catching it early is key!

question: Why are children with acute osteomyelitis at risk for long-term bone growth issues?

options.A: Bones in children never fully heal once inflamed
options.B: Antibiotics used in pediatrics actively dissolve healthy cartilage
options.C: Children lack any ability to form new bone after an infection
options.D: The infection can damage nearby growth plates, altering future bone growth

explanation: Kids are still growing! If an infection spreads into their growth plates (epiphyseal plates), it can mess with how that bone grows as they get older.
